To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the fluorescence intensity and lifetime of PI and EB are sensitive to chromatin structure and can be used to detect changes in chromatin structure in fixed cells.
D2O enhances both the intensity and lifetime of the fluorochrome PI bound to nucleic acids and fixed cells.
the fluorescence lifetime of PI and EB intercalated into DNA is sensitive to chromosomal structure and can be used to differentiate between cells with different chromosomal structure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of flow cytometric techniques for the study of chromatin structure.
the use of D2O to enhance the fluorescence lifetime of intercalating dyes and the subsequent application of this technology to flow cytometry for the detection of apoptosis and DNA damage.
the application of phase-sensitive flow cytometric analysis to the detection of changes in the fluorescence lifetime of intercalating DNA probes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of deuterium oxide in fluorescence lifetime flow cytometric measurements of DNA-bound fluorochromes can lead to erroneous interpretations of the data.
the fluorescence lifetime is a very sensitive parameter for detecting differences in DNA structure and chromatin configuration.
the fluorescence lifetime of intercalating probes is sensitive to changes in the chromatin structure and can be used as a measure of changes in chromatin configuration.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the fluorescence intensity and lifetime of intercalating DNA probes are sensitive to changes in DNA structure and chromatin state and can be used to differentiate between cell types and subpopulations of cells.
the fluorescence lifetime of PI and EB is sensitive to changes in the DNA conformation and that D2O can be used to enhance the signal intensity and lifetime of PI and/or EB.

D2O increases the fluorescence intensity of PI or EB bound to DNA by increasing the number of excited molecules that emit fluorescence, and that D2O decreases the fluorescence lifetime of PI and EB by decreasing the number of excited PI and EB molecules that decay via the fluorescence pathway.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of deuterium oxide in fluorescence lifetime flow cytometric studies of DNA structure and chromatin configuration is a useful approach for the study of DNA-protein interactions.
the use of D2O can provide additional information on the interactions of intercalating probes with DNA and chromatin structures in fixed cells.
the fluorescence intensity and lifetime of intercalating probes are sensitive to chromatin structure and that these probes can be used to study chromatin configuration and structure in cells.
